lesson.menu_desc: Holding two opposing ideas in one sentence without breaking it in the middle -- 32 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 12 -- Sounding Educated
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Gustavo Marinho de Carvalho | Lesson 12 -- Sounding Educated

listenings.text: There is a simple reason why some people sound more educated in a second language than others, and it has very little to do with vocabulary. It is the length of the thought. A speaker who only has and, but and because has to stop every six or seven words and start again, so even a clever idea arrives in small pieces. A speaker who also has although, whereas and despite can hold two opposing ideas in the same sentence, and that is exactly what an educated argument sounds like. Yes, this is true, and at the same time, this other thing is also true. You do not need difficult words to do it. You need about five small connectors, and the confidence to keep the sentence going until the second half arrives.

Our city closed the main street to cars two years ago, and I was against it. I drove to work every day, and I was sure the shops would lose customers. Although I still drive, I have to admit that I was mostly wrong. The shops did not close. In fact, despite the complaints in the first few months, most of them now have more people walking past than before. However, it has not been good for everybody. Small businesses that depend on deliveries say their costs have gone up, whereas the cafes and restaurants are doing better than ever. So when people ask me now whether it was a good idea, I give the answer I like least. It depends on who you ask.

reading.rtitle: The Four-Day Week, Two Years Later
paras: A few years ago, the four-day week sounded like a fantasy. Today, although it is still rare, it is no longer strange. Hundreds of companies in several countries have run a trial, usually for six months, in which staff worked four days a week for the same salary.

The result everybody quotes is the first one: productivity mostly stayed the same, whereas sick days and reports of burnout fell. Most of the companies not only kept the new schedule after the trial ended, but also said that hiring had become easier.

Despite these results, many economists remain skeptical. Their concern is not that the trials were dishonest. It is that the companies that volunteered were the ones most likely to succeed: small, office-based and already flexible. That is a real limit on the evidence. A factory or a hospital cannot simply close on Fridays.

So the honest answer is neither yes nor no. In some jobs, the benefits clearly outweigh the costs. In others, the same idea would mean longer shifts on the remaining four days, which is not obviously more sustainable. The interesting question is no longer whether it works. It is where.
reading.source: Written for this lesson. The claims are general and reflect what has been widely reported about four-day week trials.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: The four-day week has failed in most of the companies that tried it.
The trials look positive, but they come mostly from the easiest companies, so the real question is which jobs it suits.
Economists now agree that every company, including factories and hospitals, should move to a four-day week as soon as it can.
